The laundromat had a clock that ran eleven minutes fast. Everyone knew this except new customers, who occasionally stood up in alarm.

Mara liked it. There were few places left where you could be late and then discover you weren’t.

She came on Thursdays with two bags: clothes in the blue one, everything that required a gentler cycle in the green. At home, these categories seemed obvious. Under the laundromat’s fluorescent lights, she reconsidered them. A sweater could go either way. So could most things.

The man who cleaned the machines was kneeling beside dryer six.

“Broken?” she asked.

“Something in the drum.”

He reached into the narrow space with a pair of long pliers and withdrew a small brass key.

“Yours?”

She shook her head.

He laid it on the folding table. There were already three buttons there and a foreign coin.

“What do you do with all that?”

“Keep it for a while.”

“How long?”

He considered the key.

“Longer for keys.”

Mara put her clothes in the washer. Outside, a bus stopped without letting anyone off. The driver sat with both hands resting on the wheel, looking into the laundromat. Then the doors folded shut.

For six months, Mara had carried a key to an apartment she no longer lived in. Returning it would require either an envelope or a conversation. She had bought envelopes. They were in a drawer beneath the takeaway menus.

She touched the key through the lining of her coat.

The man had moved on to dryer seven. He wiped the inside of the door, turning the cloth to find a clean patch.

“Ever find anything good?” she asked.

“Forty dollars.”

“Did someone come back?”

“Yes.”

“Oh.”

He looked over his shoulder.

“They were pretty happy.”

When her washing finished, Mara transferred it to two dryers, keeping the sweater separate. She stayed until everything was dry, though the clock said she should already have left.

At the folding table, she picked up the brass key. Its teeth were packed with grey lint. She scraped them clean with a thumbnail and set it back beside the buttons.

Then she folded her clothes while the man switched off the machines along the empty wall.
